title: The question about caste
hookLine: a boy who tells a teacher the plain truth about not knowing his father, and the question a classmate asks today
carry: satya: the door opened for truth, not birth
last: EVEN RAMA ASKED THE MOTHER FIRST.

cards: A boy wants to study with a well-known teacher, and the first thing a teacher will ask is his family line. So he goes to his mother: who is my father? Her answer is brave.

When she was young, she says, she worked as a servant, moving from house to house, and she doesn't know. Tell him you're Satyakama, son of Jabala. So the boy walks to the teacher's door and says exactly that.
And everyone waits to see if the door shuts. A version of that moment still happens, in a classroom, when someone asks: isn't Hinduism just the caste system?

teach.h: ONLY A TRUE BRAHMIN SPEAKS SUCH TRUTH.
teach.b: Here's how the old story ends. The teacher listens and says: only a true brahmin would speak such truth. Bring the firewood; I'll teach you.
One of the oldest Upanishads tells it; people have argued about it since. Some hear birth being set aside for honesty. Others notice the teacher still reaches for the old label.
Both readings are honest. Now the hard part, plainly. The English word caste comes from Portuguese, casta, a lineage.
It lumps together two Indian ideas. Varna is the four classes the old texts describe: priests and teachers, rulers and warriors, traders and farmers, and workers.
In the Gita, Krishna says the four were made by quality and action. Jati means birth, and it's the word for the thousands of communities people are actually born into. Over centuries, birth won.

teach.h: BIRTH WON, AND PEOPLE WERE HURT.
teach.b: Families were ranked, some people were treated as untouchable, and real harm was done, and in places it still is. Many Hindus pushed back, too. The poet-saint Ravidas, a leatherworker by trade, is still sung and honored.
B. R. Ambedkar, born into a family treated as untouchable, fought caste fiercely and helped write India's constitution, which abolished untouchability.
Hindus today still disagree about what varna was ever meant to be, and your family and your teachers may see it differently. So what do you say in the classroom? Something true.
Caste is real, it hurt people, and many Hindus reject ranking anyone by birth.

teach.h: SAY WHAT'S TRUE, THEN WHAT YOU STAND FOR.
teach.b: Then say what you stand for.
Satyakama got through the door with one thing: satya, truth. Start there.

how: Hindus hold many views on caste: many reject ranking by birth outright, some read varna as temperament and calling, and families and teachers differ; untouchability is abolished by India's constitution.

games.q: a classmate asks, not unkindly: isn't Hinduism just the caste system? what's a true answer?
o: caste never existed; outsiders made it up.
caste is real and hurt people; many Hindus reject ranking by birth, and here's what I stand for.
change the subject and hope they forget.
games.why: you don't have to deny the history or defend it. like Satyakama, start with satya, truth: say what's true, then what you stand for.

practice: First, a time someone decided who you were before you spoke, by your name, your accent, your skin, your family; feel how small that box was.

Then, if one comes, a time you did the same to someone else; no need to punish yourself, just see it. Satyakama walked to the teacher's door with nothing but the truth; let that be enough for this sit.

wordCard.voice: Jati. Birth: the community a person is born into, and most of what people mean by caste.

orig.note: Sanskrit and Hindi: birth, and the birth community; most of what people mean by caste.

carryVoice: Your line: satya: the door opened for truth, not birth. Say what's true, then what you stand for. That's ninety-five.
